title: The traveling scholars
hook: scholars journeyed far to hear one hadith from its source

segments.voice: Yesterday, rijal, the science of men, and your line: who was he? Did you look up who first said something before you shared it? Day one thousand one hundred fifty.

One line in Sahih al-Bukhari, almost tucked away in a chapter heading. Jabir ibn Abdullah, a companion of the Prophet ﷺ, traveled a month's distance to Abdullah ibn Unays, for a single hadith. Not for trade. Not for war. One report. Fuller tellings of the story, outside Bukhari, add the details: Jabir buys a camel, saddles up, and rides to hear the report himself rather than take it secondhand. A month on the road, for one report. Today, the traveling scholars.
screen: `A MONTH'S DISTANCE.` → `FOR A SINGLE HADITH.` → `NOT SECONDHAND.`

segments.voice: First, the chapter. In Sahih al-Bukhari, in the Book of Knowledge, the chapter on going out in search of knowledge names Jabir's journey, and the report placed beneath it is about a prophet. Moses went looking for a man with knowledge he didn't have. The Qur'an gives his resolve, in Pickthall's words: "I will not give up until I reach the point where the two rivers meet, though I march on for ages." A companion, and a prophet, in one chapter. Travel for learning sits in old company. Second, why not take it secondhand? Because every link in the chain is a place for something to slip, as the scholars knew. If you can hear it from the person who heard it, the chain gets shorter and the path gets clearer. Scholars of hadith prized a shorter chain, and some traveled for that alone. Third, the journey became a tradition of its own. Students moved between cities to sit with the teachers there, to compare what they'd heard, to check a report against another chain. The journey even has a name, rihla, and the scholar al-Khatib al-Baghdadi wrote a book gathering these journeys in search of hadith. Fourth, what they carried home. Not souvenirs. Notebooks. And the habit behind them is spelled out in a hadith in Sahih Muslim: whoever travels a road seeking knowledge, Allah makes easy for him a road to paradise. By that hadith, the road to learning is itself counted.
screen: `A COMPANION, AND A PROPHET.` · `WHY NOT SECONDHAND?` · `RIHLA: THE JOURNEY FOR HADITH.` · `A ROAD MADE EASY.`

segments.voice: The practice: travel to learn. Settle, and breathe. Is there something you've been taking secondhand? A question about your faith, your family's history, your work, that you've only ever heard about from people who heard it from someone else. Who holds it firsthand? A teacher, an elder, a grandparent, a scholar at the mosque or the library across town? Choose one. Now plan the journey, even if it's twenty minutes on a bus or a phone call across an ocean. When could you go? What one question would you bring? If you pray, you can ask for an easy road. The bell holds the time.
The traveling scholars. Companions and students who rode far to hear a report from its source, so the chain would be shorter and surer. Today's word.

Your line: a journey for one report. Today, take the first step of the journey you planned: send the message, check the time, ask the question. Tomorrow: exposing the fabrications. Day one thousand one hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Students of hadith and Islamic learning have long traveled to study with teachers in person, a practice called the rihla, and some still travel to receive a chain of transmission directly from a teacher.
